name: The Light We Borrow
description: A lullaby that has existed in so many versions across so many GLMZ communities since its first documented appearance in 2189 that its original form is essentially unrecoverable. What all versions share is a descending five-note melodic figure — clean, slow, immediately memorable — and a lyric structure in which a parent or caregiver tells a child that the light coming through whatever window they can see is borrowed from somewhere warmer and will be returned someday. Shelf versions tend to be unaccompanied or sung over a single sustained drone. Circuit versions add simple percussion. A Tier 3 commercial recording by Amara Solís-Nakamura in 2204 became the best-selling single in GLMZ history, though Shelf residents largely consider that version a dilution.
creator: Traditional (various); commercial version by Amara Solís-Nakamura
distributor: Vantablack Media subsidiary (commercial version); oral tradition (original)
audience: Children and parents across all tiers; the oral tradition version is Tier 1-2, the Solís-Nakamura recording is Tier 2-4, neural-feed arrangements exist for Tier 4-5 nurseries
cultural_impact: The song's ubiquity makes it one of the few genuine cross-tier cultural touchstones in GLMZ — a Spire executive and a Shelf child know the same melody, even if their versions' words are different. This has made it simultaneously beloved and contested: Vantablack Media's copyright claim on the Solís-Nakamura arrangement technically extends to 'derivatives,' a legal gray area that community singers in the Shelf have simply ignored. Scholars of M88 culture note that the song's central metaphor — borrowed light, temporary warmth, an implicit promise of return — resonates differently depending on which tier you're singing it in, and that the same five notes carry entirely different weights of hope and grief depending on the window you're looking through.
known_fans: Tier 3 and 4 families who know the Solís-Nakamura version
music historians studying cross-tier cultural transmission
neural-feed composers who have built arrangements on the melodic figure
story_hooks: A researcher studying oral tradition in the Shelf discovers a version of the lullaby with an extra verse that appears nowhere in any recording — the verse describes, in plain language, a specific location in the city that should not exist.

Vantablack Media begins aggressively enforcing its copyright claim against Shelf community singers, sending cease-and-desist notices to parents; the players are drawn into what begins as a legal aid case and becomes something larger.
A Tier 5 child is found wandering in the Shelf, unable to explain how she got there, singing the Shelf version of the lullaby — a version she could not have learned in the Spire.
